title: Bangla Sahib
hook: in Delhi, the gurdwara of the child Guru, with its healing pool

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Akal Takht, new stone on old ground, facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Your line was facing each other.

A plastic bottle, the kind you'd buy at any corner shop, sits on a kitchen shelf in a Delhi apartment. Nobody drinks from it casually. It was filled at the edge of a pool in the middle of the city, carried home on the metro, and kept for when someone in the house is unwell. A grandmother pours a little into a steel cup and hands it over without a word. The pool is at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, near one of the city's big traffic circles. Year one told how the child Guru came to Delhi. Today, the place he left behind, and the water.
screen: `A BOTTLE ON A KITCHEN SHELF.` → `KEPT FOR WHEN SOMEONE IS UNWELL.` → `FILLED AT A POOL IN DELHI.`

segments.voice: First, the house. Bangla means bungalow. Tradition says Guru Har Krishan, the eighth Guru and still a child, stayed here in the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh when he was called to Delhi. While he was there, an epidemic swept the city, and the child went out among the sick of every faith. He caught the disease himself and died in Delhi. The bungalow became a gurdwara. Second, the water. Tradition says the house's well gave the water the young Guru blessed and handed to the sick. Today a wide pool, a sarovar, lies beside the gurdwara, and people sit by it, touch the water to their eyes, and fill bottles to take home. Some Sikhs add a caution: the water isn't a charm; what it carries is the memory of a child who served. Third, a hymn. In Raag Sorath, Guru Arjan gives thanks, in paraphrase: the Beloved has given protection from smallpox; the Supreme Lord has shown mercy. Tradition links that hymn to Guru Arjan's young son, the boy who would become Guru Hargobind, when he fell ill. So, as tradition reads it, the Granth holds a father's relief over a sick child. At Bangla Sahib the story turns around: here it's the child who goes to the sick. Fourth, Sikhs say the same light passed from Guru to Guru, whatever the body's age. At Bangla Sahib you can see what that light did in a small body: it didn't hide from a sick city.
screen: `BANGLA: A RAJA'S BUNGALOW.` · `A POOL FOR THOSE WHO ARE UNWELL.` · `GURU ARJAN'S THANKS FOR A SICK CHILD.` · `THE LIGHT IN A SMALL BODY.` · then, large: `THE CHILD'S GURDWARA.`

segments.voice: See the wide water, the white building and the gold dome, the steps going down to the edge, and people sitting quietly, someone filling a bottle for a person at home. Now bring to mind one person you know who is unwell, and sit beside them in your mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can rest on Waheguru.
Bangla Sahib. The gurdwara in Delhi at the bungalow where tradition says Guru Har Krishan stayed and served the sick, with its pool beside it. Today's word.
Your line: the child's gurdwara. The pool still holds the memory of a child who went to the sick. That's today's step.

Ang 620 (Sorath M5, 'seetlaa te rakhiaa bihaaree, paarbraham prabh kirpaa dhaaree') is traditionally linked to the child Hargobind's recovery from smallpox. Please confirm Ang and that the tradition links it to Hargobind.
'Sikhs speak of it carefully: the water itself is not a medicine' is a fair-sounding summary of Sikh teaching against charms, but not sourced; please confirm the wording.

The hook (bottles filled at the sarovar and kept at home for the sick) is a general description of practice; please confirm it is fair. 'A short walk from one of the city's big traffic circles' means as Connaught Place but is not named; cut if inaccurate.
'Bangla means bungalow' was also stated on day 689.
